label: Computational irreducibility makes short theorems with only long proofs inevitable
claim: Because the proof processes of almost every area of mathematics are computationally irreducible, adding axioms cannot remove the problem: there will essentially always be theorems that are short to state but whose shortest proofs are very long.
quote: But I suspect that ultimately there is almost always computational irreducibility, and this makes it essentially inevitable that there will be short theorems that only allow long proofs.
scope: axiom systems of mathematics, idealized as multiway systems
measurable_quantities: statement length versus shortest proof length across theorems of an axiom system
growth of the maximum shortest-proof length as a function of statement length
candidate_data: Formal proof libraries such as Metamath set.mm, Lean mathlib and the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs, together with automated theorem provers, give statement and proof sizes; explicit enumeration of small multiway systems is feasible.

label: An irreducible multiway system cannot be both complete and consistent
claim: If questions about the long-run evolution of a multiway system (an idealized axiom system) are undecidable, then the system cannot be both complete and consistent, because completeness plus consistency would give a procedure that always terminates to decide whether a string is reached.
quote: So the result of this is that if the evolution of a multiway system is computationally irreducible—so that questions about its ultimate behavior are undecidable—the system cannot be both complete and consistent.
scope: multiway systems interpreted as axiom systems with a negation operation
candidate_data: Standard computability-theory results bear on it; it is checkable by proof rather than data.

label: Gödel's Theorem follows from the universality of arithmetic, shown via rule 110
claim: An integer (exponential Diophantine) equation can be built whose solutions emulate the rule 110 cellular automaton; since rule 110 is universal, the axioms of arithmetic support universality, which implies Gödel's Theorem that arithmetic contains statements that cannot be proved true or false. Wolfram presents Gödel's Theorem as a consequence of the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
quote: And with the cellular automaton being a universal one such as rule 110 this implies that the axioms of arithmetic can support universality.
scope: axioms of integer arithmetic (Peano arithmetic) and Diophantine encodings of cellular automata
measurable_quantities: correctness of the Diophantine encoding of rule 110 evolution
universality of rule 110
candidate_data: The published literature on Gödel incompleteness and on Diophantine representations of computation (Hilbert's Tenth Problem) bears on it, and the encoding can be checked by computer algebra.

label: Beyond a low threshold almost every axiom system should be universal
claim: The Principle of Computational Equivalence implies that, beyond a low threshold of complexity, almost any axiom system (including very simple ones) should be universal, and so should exhibit undecidability and have no general upper limit on proof length.
quote: And indeed the Principle of Computational Equivalence implies that beyond some low threshold almost any axiom system should be expected to be universal.
scope: all axiom systems, including simple operator and multiway systems
measurable_quantities: fraction of enumerated simple axiom systems that can be shown universal or undecidable
candidate_data: Enumeration of small equational axiom systems with automated provers and model finders (e.g. Prover9/Mace4) bears on it, though proving universality case by case is hard.

label: Every axiom system used in current mathematical research is universal
claim: Basic logic and pure predicate logic are not universal, but adding a function or relation with more than one argument gives universality; arithmetic, set theory, group theory and ring theory are universal, and every axiom system actually used in current mathematical research is known to be universal, while heavily constrained systems such as commutative group theory and simplified real algebra and geometry are not.
quote: But of the axiom systems actually used in current mathematics research every single one is now known to be universal.
scope: standard axiom systems of mathematics (logic, predicate logic, arithmetic, set theory, group theory, ring theory, real algebra, geometry)
measurable_quantities: decidability or undecidability status of each theory
candidate_data: The established mathematical-logic literature on decidable and undecidable first-order theories (e.g. Tarski on real closed fields, Tarski–Mostowski–Robinson on undecidable theories) bears on it.

label: Simple integer equations should exist whose lack of solutions is unprovable
claim: Although known universal integer equations are very complicated (the simplest having 9 variables and an immense number of terms), there should be much simpler integer equations for which the absence of solutions can never be proved from the standard axioms of arithmetic.
quote: so that in fact there are in the end rather simple integer equations for which the absence of solutions can never be proved from the normal axioms of arithmetic.
scope: Diophantine equations and Peano arithmetic
measurable_quantities: size (variables, degree, terms) of the smallest known universal or independent Diophantine equation
candidate_data: The literature on universal Diophantine equations and on smallest-solution searches for small equations bears on it, as does computational searching of equation families.

label: Many open number-theory problems may be unprovable from arithmetic's axioms
claim: A fair fraction of the unsolved problems seriously studied in number theory will turn out to be questions that cannot be answered using the standard axioms of arithmetic.
quote: And it is my strong suspicion that in fact of all the current unsolved problems seriously studied in number theory a fair fraction will in the end turn out to be questions that cannot ever be answered using the normal axioms of arithmetic.
scope: open problems in number theory relative to Peano arithmetic
measurable_quantities: fraction of open number-theory problems later resolved within Peano arithmetic versus shown independent
candidate_data: Lists of open problems (e.g. Guy's Unsolved Problems in Number Theory) and the record of their resolution over time bear on it.

label: Undecidability appears in almost any area of mathematics beyond easy questions
claim: Undecidability and unprovability will begin to occur in practically any area of mathematics almost as soon as one goes beyond questions that are always easy to answer, as a consequence of the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
quote: And indeed from the Principle of Computational Equivalence I strongly believe that in general undecidability and unprovability will start to occur in practically any area of mathematics almost as soon as one goes beyond the level of questions that are always easy to answer.
scope: all areas of mathematics
measurable_quantities: incidence of undecidability or independence results across mathematical fields
candidate_data: Surveys of known undecidability and independence results across fields bear on it only partially.

label: Mathematics avoids undecidability by choosing questions its methods can answer
claim: Undecidability and unprovability have seemed rare in mathematics because mathematics, shaped by its history, has defined itself around the questions and systems that proof-based methods can address, concentrating on limited patches of computational reducibility; so present-day mathematics is a small and uncharacteristic sample of what is possible.
quote: it is that like most other fields of human inquiry mathematics has tended to define itself to be concerned with just those questions that its methods can successfully address.
scope: the practice and history of mathematics
candidate_data: none known

label: Complete and consistent means exactly half of all strings are generated
claim: For a multiway system serving as an axiom system, with negation any length-preserving involution on strings, the system is complete and consistent exactly when half of all possible strings of each length are eventually generated from the string representing true; more than half implies inconsistency and less than half implies incompleteness.
quote: the criterion for whether a system is complete and consistent is simply that exactly half the possible strings of a given length are eventually generated if one starts from the string representing "true".
scope: multiway systems treated as axiom systems with length-preserving negation
measurable_quantities: fraction of strings of each length generated by a multiway system
candidate_data: Direct enumeration of multiway systems with standard software can confirm the criterion and its consequences.

label: Axiom systems used in mathematics are usually close to complete
claim: The axiom systems widely used in mathematics, though usually incomplete, are typically close to complete, because they were built to describe definite kinds of objects; as a result, the alternative objects (nonstandard models) that also satisfy them, such as those for standard arithmetic, differ only in obscure ways.
quote: For if one looks at axiom systems that are widely used in mathematics they almost all tend to be complete enough to prove at least a fair fraction of statements either true or false.
scope: standard axiom systems of mathematics such as arithmetic, group theory and set theory
measurable_quantities: fraction of enumerated short statements an axiom system proves or refutes
candidate_data: Automated theorem provers applied to enumerated short statements of a theory could estimate this; benchmark libraries such as TPTP exist.

label: Most simple axiom systems admit many different operator forms
claim: Enumerating simple axiom systems for a binary operator shows that the vast majority allow operators of many different forms (many models), so they are not about any one particular operator and are far from complete; only a few, such as those for logic, force essentially a single form.
quote: But what the pictures on the next two pages [804, 805] show is that the vast majority of axiom systems actually allow operators with all sorts of different forms.
scope: simple equational axiom systems for a single binary operator
measurable_quantities: number of non-isomorphic models with 2, 3 and 4 elements for each enumerated axiom system
candidate_data: Finite model finders such as Mace4 and existing enumerations of small magmas, semigroups and groups (e.g. in GAP or OEIS) can reproduce the counts.

label: Very short single-axiom systems for logic exist among the simplest axiom systems
claim: Propositional logic can be axiomatized in terms of Nand by a single axiom with only six Nands (found by searching small axiom systems), far shorter than textbook systems, so an axiom system for logic is likely to be found among the simplest few thousand axiom systems.
quote: So what this means is that if one were just to go through a list of the simplest few thousand axiom systems one would already be quite likely to find one that represents logic.
scope: equational axiom systems for Boolean algebra in terms of Nand
measurable_quantities: size of the shortest single axiom for Nand-based Boolean algebra
rank of the first working axiom system in an enumeration
candidate_data: Automated provers such as Otter/Prover9 can verify the proofs, and the published literature on single axioms for Boolean algebra bears on it.

label: Traditional axiom systems are not fundamentally special; others could found new fields
claim: Apart from history, nothing fundamentally distinguishes the axiom systems traditionally used in mathematics (logic included), and many other axiom systems, often simple ones, could serve as foundations for new fields of mathematics as rich as the traditional ones.
quote: So this leads to the conclusion that there is in a sense nothing fundamentally special about the particular axiom systems that have traditionally been used in mathematics
scope: axiom systems underlying fields of mathematics
candidate_data: none known

label: Named textbook theorems of logic are those not derivable from simpler ones
claim: If the theorems of basic logic are listed in order of increasing complexity, the ones that cannot be derived from simpler theorems earlier in the list are almost exactly the ones traditional textbooks single out and name as interesting.
quote: And remarkably enough what I have found is that these theorems are almost exactly the ones highlighted on the previous page that have traditionally been identified as interesting.
scope: theorems of propositional logic and the named laws in logic textbooks
measurable_quantities: overlap between theorems not derivable from earlier ones and the named textbook theorems
candidate_data: Enumerating logic theorems with automated provers and comparing with named laws in standard logic textbooks would test it.

label: Judgments like deep or powerful reflect the structure of the theorem network
claim: Mathematicians' intuitive descriptions of theorems (difficult, powerful, surprising, deep) reflect features of the network of statements connected by theorems, and fields regarded as more successful should have more compact networks while fields full of isolated facts, such as elementary number theory, should have sparser networks.
quote: And my suspicion is that our intuitive characterizations of theorems are in effect just reflections of our perception of various features of the structure of this network.
scope: networks of theorems and proofs in fields of mathematics
measurable_quantities: dependency-graph metrics (density, reuse of lemmas, path lengths) per field
correlation of graph features with human ratings of theorems
candidate_data: Dependency graphs from formal libraries such as Lean mathlib, Metamath set.mm and the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs could be analysed.

label: No general definition of intelligence independent of human details
claim: General features proposed as marks of intelligence (learning and memory, adaptation, abstraction) occur in systems such as simple cellular automata and fluids, so there is no workable general definition of intelligence; any usable one must be tied to specific details of human intelligence.
quote: My guess is that ultimately there is not, and that in fact any workable definition of what we normally think of as intelligence will end up having to be tied to all sorts of seemingly rather specific details of human intelligence.
scope: definitions of intelligence
candidate_data: none known

label: Proposed general features of life occur in many simple-rule systems
claim: Almost any general feature proposed to characterize life, including self-organization, self-reproduction and complexity, occurs even in many systems with very simple rules, so life can only be recognized by specific shared details with life on Earth.
quote: Indeed, following the discoveries in this book I have come to the conclusion that almost any general feature that one might think of as characterizing life will actually occur even in many systems with very simple rules.
scope: definitions of life, terrestrial and extraterrestrial
measurable_quantities: presence of self-reproduction or self-organization in simple cellular automata
candidate_data: Simulations of simple cellular automata (e.g. additive rules such as rule 90) show the features; the definitional part is not empirical.

label: Human artifacts look simple because engineering requires predictability
claim: Human-made artifacts tend to look simpler than natural objects because engineers need to foresee what their systems will do, which requires computational reducibility, whereas nature has no such constraint and many natural systems are computationally irreducible.
quote: And I believe the basic answer to this has to do with the fact that when we as humans set up artifacts we usually need to be able to foresee what they will do—for otherwise we have no way to tell whether they will achieve the purposes we want.
scope: human engineering artifacts compared with natural objects
measurable_quantities: complexity or compressibility of artifact forms versus natural forms
candidate_data: Image collections of artifacts and natural objects analysed with compression-based complexity measures could bear on the comparison but not on the explanation.

label: A minimal rule for a feature hints that a system was made for a purpose
claim: Since purposes can always be reinterpreted as mechanisms, purpose cannot be identified for certain from behavior; the best criterion is that a system is the minimal or optimal one producing a given feature, which suggests it was built for that purpose, as advanced technology should increasingly use minimal systems.
quote: finding out that the rule for the system is the minimal or optimal one for producing that feature may make it seem more likely that at least with sufficiently advanced technology the system might have specifically been created for the purpose of exhibiting that feature.
scope: recognizing purpose in artifacts and signals, including extraterrestrial ones
candidate_data: none known

label: Efficient extraterrestrial communications would show no detectable regularities
claim: Signals used for communication by an advanced extraterrestrial civilization would likely be compressed to the point of showing essentially no detectable regularities, so they would look like random radio noise, and searches for sharply defined carrier frequencies would miss them; only beacons meant to be noticed would need recognizable regularities.
quote: my guess is that they will exhibit essentially no detectable regularities. For any such regularity represents in a sense a redundancy or inefficiency that can be removed by the sender and receiver both using appropriate data compression.
scope: extraterrestrial radio signals and searches for extraterrestrial intelligence
measurable_quantities: statistical regularity or compressibility of received astronomical radio signals
candidate_data: Breakthrough Listen public data releases and other radio survey archives contain broadband signals that could be analysed, though no ground truth exists.

label: Sophisticated computation, or primes, are not signs of intelligence
claim: Producing a signal by sophisticated computation is no evidence of intelligence, because such computation is common in ordinary physical processes; for instance, turbulence in the gas around a star quickly does more computation than all of human intellectual history, and sequences such as the primes can be generated by many non-intelligent systems.
quote: And indeed it seems likely that for example an ordinary physical process like fluid turbulence in the gas around a star should rather quickly do more computation than has by most measures ever been done throughout the whole course of human intellectual history.
scope: criteria for detecting extraterrestrial intelligence; natural physical processes
measurable_quantities: estimated computational capacity (e.g. operations per second) of stellar-atmosphere turbulence versus cumulative human computation
candidate_data: Turbulence simulations and estimates of degrees of freedom in stellar convection, plus estimates of historical human computation, could inform the comparison.

label: Recognizing extraterrestrial intelligence depends on similarity to humans
claim: The difficulty in finding extraterrestrial intelligence is not finding systems that compute in sophisticated ways, which are common, but finding ones whose details are similar enough to humans that we would recognize them as intelligent; somewhat generalized intelligence is likely to exist but to behave in bizarrely unhuman ways.
quote: that the basic issue is not finding systems that perform sophisticated enough computations, but rather finding ones whose details happen to be similar enough to us as humans that we recognize what they do as showing intelligence.
scope: extraterrestrial intelligence
candidate_data: none known

label: Engineering has explored only a tiny unrepresentative fraction of possible systems
claim: Traditional engineering has used only a tiny and unrepresentative fraction of possible systems and processes, those simple enough to predict, and using simple-rule systems with complex behavior will make a vast amount of new technology possible.
quote: And indeed one of the things that emerges from this book is that traditional engineering has actually considered only a tiny and quite unrepresentative fraction of all the kinds of systems and processes that are in principle possible.
scope: engineering and technology
candidate_data: Patent databases could in principle track uptake of cellular-automaton-based or searched-program technologies, but the claim is broad.

label: Simple universal rules like rule 110 could be built into computers from atoms
claim: Since very simple rules such as the rule 110 cellular automaton are universal, computers could be built from many kinds of components, and a simple chemical process could plausibly assemble a rule 110-like computer at the atomic scale, with one or a few atoms per cell.
quote: For while it is quite implausible that some simple chemical process could successfully assemble a traditional computer out of atoms, it seems quite plausible that this could be done for something like a rule 110 cellular automaton.
scope: molecular and atomic-scale computing technology
measurable_quantities: demonstrated physical implementations of universal cellular automata at molecular scale
candidate_data: The experimental literature on DNA tile self-assembly and molecular cellular automata bears on it.

label: Exhaustive search is the only reliable way to find programs with given behavior
claim: Because simple programs can do so many unexpected things, and computational irreducibility can make finding a behavior take irreducible work, the only reliable way to find a simple program with a desired behavior is essentially exhaustive search, so building a library of basic knowledge about simple programs is a better route to technology.
quote: ultimately the only way to find what one wants is essentially just to do an exhaustive search of all possibilities.
scope: design of simple programs for technological purposes
measurable_quantities: success rates of exhaustive versus iterative or evolutionary search for programs with specified behavior
candidate_data: Benchmarks in program synthesis and evolutionary computation, and enumerations of cellular automaton rule spaces, could be compared.

label: Humans are not computationally more sophisticated than other systems in nature
claim: By the Principle of Computational Equivalence, human brains, turbulent fluids, simple cellular automata and the universe as a whole all achieve the same level of computational sophistication, so humans are not fundamentally special in intelligence or complexity.
quote: So this means that there is in the end no difference between the level of computational sophistication that is achieved by humans and by all sorts of other systems in nature and elsewhere.
scope: humans, natural systems, simple programs and the universe
candidate_data: none known

label: Computational irreducibility puts permanent limits on scientific prediction
claim: The Principle of Computational Equivalence and computational irreducibility show that science will never predict everything: even if the universe follows simple rules, there is in general no way to know all their consequences except by watching them unfold.
quote: But the Principle of Computational Equivalence—and the phenomenon of computational irreducibility—now shows that this will never happen.
scope: science and knowledge in general
candidate_data: none known
